fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title":"The Dogma Beneath Every Trauma","body":"Chance frames the episode around beliefs about health that were inherited so early and reinforced so consistently that they stopped registering as beliefs at all, noting that even the scientific establishment concedes germ theory is theory rather than proven law. Dalton, who came through a master's program in microbiology and virology before moving into counseling psychology, says the admission that we sometimes do not know is what kept him grounded among professors and colleagues. Both men argue that the most invisible trauma is dogma itself, the instruction to defer to experts, and Chance ties inner knowing to conscience, citing his previous interview with Dr. Edith Ubuntu Chan."},{"title":"Relinquishing The Therapy License","body":"Dalton recounts the complaints filed against his Beyond Terrain work with the regulatory college that governed therapy in his province, the meetings and back and forth, and the demand that he delete all his content, all while his wife was pregnant and he was twenty five. He describes hundreds of thousands of dollars spent on education, a practice and advertising, plus a belief that he was not good enough which his EMDR, somatic experiencing and nervous system regulation training kept circling back to. One morning he decided to stop believing it, sent an email relinquishing his license, and says his academy took off that same week."},{"title":"Conditioned Adaptation Not Brokenness","body":"Both men reject the idea that trauma explains outcomes, pointing out that two people can live through the same event and land in completely different lives, one developing cancer and one passing gracefully in their sleep at a hundred. Dalton compares that inconsistency to asymptomatic cases under germ theory, and cites Owen Benjamin's book How to Slay a Wizard on the greatest lie, that you are not enough, alongside Carl Jung on the tree whose roots reach hell. Chance reframes trauma as conditioned adaptation rather than brokenness, and Dalton recalls copying an older kid's laugh in grade ten and keeping it for years without noticing."},{"title":"A Thought Carried Through Time","body":"Dalton brings in Sydney Banks and the short book The Enlightened Gardener to argue that feeling follows thought, so trauma is nothing but a thought carried through time and analyzing it only deepens the suffering. He points to what the three principles world calls a psychological immune system, then extends the logic to the body, describing his infant daughter's eye discharge at a month old, the proton pump inhibitors given to babies with reflux, and his friend Wes Rowe's son, who he says leapt ahead cognitively after a fever nobody suppressed. Dalton contends there is no disease in nature, only adaptation and self-correction."},{"title":"No Parasites In Nature","body":"Turning to parasites, Dalton traces the Greek root meaning he who eats at another man's table and claims the parasitic relationship does not exist in nature, only allowance, illustrating it with the Seinfeld episode where Jerry finally says no to Kramer. He applies the same argument to Hayek, Mises and Hoppe in Austrian economics, who cast government as parasite, notes that the Amish pay no taxes, and recalls a Mi'kmaq language course with no words for greed, jealousy or gluttony. Chance counters with ticks killing moose where predator populations are thinned, as in Missouri, and both urge listeners to abandon victim consciousness."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Liev Dalton of Beyond Terrain joins InnerVerse to challenge germ theory, trauma dogma, symptom suppression, supplements, protocols, and the deeper healing trap hidden inside both mainstream and alternative medicine.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: This conversation teaches terrain health, exposes fear-based stories that keep people stuck, and why true healing begins with spiritual wholeness. Liev's background in biochemistry, molecular biology, microbiology, virology, and counseling psychology gives him a unique perspective on the dogmas of both mainstream medicine and alternative healing culture. After years of working as a therapist and exploring psychosomatic modalities, Liev came to a difficult realization: many people were not being set free by endlessly focusing on their trauma, symptoms, diagnoses, supplements, and protocols. In many cases, the healing process itself had become another identity trap. The first hour gets into the philosophy of terrain medicine, the limitations of germ theory, finishing with "trauma healing" for good, Liev's departure from the regulated therapy world, and the deeper spiritual question of what it means to become whole rather than endlessly "work on" being healed. In the Plus+ extension, the conversation gets even more contrarian as Liev turns the parasite panic upside down, questioning ivermectin, deworming, parasite cleanses, supplement protocols, and the whole "kill the hidden enemy" mindset. Are parasites really the cause of disease, or are they part of the body's attempt to remediate a problem?

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Terrain Decides, Not the Organism", "body": "Liev walks through roughly seventy five human challenge papers he tracked down, studies where volunteers swallowed hookworms, whipworms, tapeworms, amoebas and Cryptosporidium, and reports that the most common outcome by far was that nothing happened at all. He points to asymptomatic rates running as high as ninety five or ninety nine percent for some organisms, and argues that if the presence of something almost never lines up with symptoms, presence cannot be the determining factor. What is left, he says, is the condition of the host, which carries the free hour's terrain argument all the way into the second."}, {"title": "Parasites as the Cleanup Crew", "body": "The reframe Liev builds rests on Thomas Dykstra's work with insects, which he says will not touch plants carrying high sugar readings and only move on plants growing in poor soil, thin light or the wrong microclimate. Insects, in that reading, are the regulatory beings of the plant world, and the same logic scales inward, with organisms taking up heavy metals at concentrations host tissue could never survive and converting oxidized metals into reduced forms. Chance runs the fractal outward, pointing out that flies land on waste because waste is exactly what needs breaking down."}, {"title": "Suppression as Biological Debt", "body": "Both men keep returning to the idea that making a symptom disappear is borrowing against the future. Liev describes the messages he gets constantly, temporary relief followed three or four months later by the same trouble coming back differently, and frames it as a model where what is pushed down simply moves rather than resolving. Chance scales the same shape up to the geopolitics of mass deworming, where the World Bank and the IMF lend to developing nations at interest and then restructure them, and lands on the line that nature never serves a free lunch."}, {"title": "How the Literature Gets Told", "body": "A long stretch of the members hour is about the papers themselves. Liev says the few studies where subjects did develop symptoms had either cleared the gut beforehand or introduced the organism alongside formalin or salt water, which he treats as an uncontrolled variable nobody accounted for. He describes sources from the eighteen hundreds being routinely miscited by modern reviews, and five hours of archive digging to locate two of them. Chance recognizes the same pattern from comparative mythology and philology, where popular writers count on nobody ever checking the receipts."}, {"title": "Attunement Over Protocols", "body": "The final stretch leaves biology for practice. Liev rejects one size fits all thinking, including the rigidity he sees in German new medicine, and describes his mentorship work as teaching people to become their own authority rather than copy somebody else's story. Chance offers cases from his tuning practice where changing a client's belief that she had to carry everyone else's problems preceded changes she had not gone looking for. Both land on water, intention and surrender, and on epiphanies as the ten or fifteen second moments where the real shift actually happens."}]
